articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.1M software contract went to firm with no public bid competitors
articles.dek: Public records show the enterprise resource planning system was sole-sourced after a requirements document matched only one vendor's specifications.
brief: Escambia County awarded a $2.1 million enterprise resource planning contract to Tyler Technologies without competitive bidding
Public records obtained by The Flightline show the county's requirements document contained specifications that matched only Tyler's Munis platform
County officials say the sole-source process was legal under Florida statutes, but good-government advocates question whether taxpayers got the best deal
articles.body:
The requirements document ran 47 pages. It specified cloud hosting architecture, module integration capabilities, Florida-specific payroll tax compliance features, and compatibility with the county's existing Kronos timekeeping system.

It also specified, on page 31, that the winning vendor must have "existing installations in at least 15 Florida counties with populations exceeding 200,000."

In the state of Florida, exactly one enterprise resource planning vendor meets that criterion: Tyler Technologies.

Escambia County's Board of County Commissioners approved the $2.1 million contract with Tyler on March 14, 2026, after a procurement process that produced zero competitive bids. Public records obtained by The Flightline through a Florida Sunshine Law request show the county never issued a formal request for proposals. Instead, administrators used a sole-source justification memo dated January 8, 2026, that cited Tyler's "unique qualifications" and existing state purchasing agreements.

How the deal happened

The county's Information Technology department began planning the ERP replacement in summer 2025. The existing system, a heavily customized installation of SAP software purchased in 2009, had become expensive to maintain and lacked modern cloud capabilities, according to budget documents.

Amy Lowenstein, the county's IT director, drafted the initial requirements document in September 2025. Internal emails show she circulated it to department heads for feedback through October, then submitted a final version to the Purchasing Department on November 12.

That document never went out for public bid.

On December 3, County Administrator Wes Moreno signed a determination memo authorizing sole-source procurement under Florida Statute 287.057(3)(c), which permits agencies to bypass competitive bidding when "only one source" can provide a required commodity or service.

"The Tyler Munis platform is the only ERP solution that meets all mandatory requirements identified by county departments," the memo states. "Competitive solicitation would serve no useful purpose."

Tyler submitted its proposal on December 18. The contract went to commissioners for approval 86 days later.

The specification question

Government procurement experts who reviewed the requirements document at The Flightline's request said several specifications appeared tailored to eliminate competition.

"That 15-county requirement is a tell," said Marcus Webb, a former procurement officer for Hillsborough County who now consults for local governments. "There's no operational reason you need a vendor who's already in 15 large Florida counties. What you need is software that works. This is spec-writing designed to get a predetermined outcome."

Webb identified three other requirements he called "unusually narrow": a mandate for the vendor's customer support center to be located within the continental United States, a requirement for "native integration" with Kronos Workforce Ready specifically, and a clause requiring the vendor to have processed Florida TRIM notices for at least five years.

Infor, Oracle, and Workday — three major ERP vendors with government divisions — all have U.S.-based support and Florida installations. None currently offers native Kronos integration. None has processed TRIM notices in Florida.

Tyler does all three.

County defends the process

In a written statement, County Administrator Moreno said the procurement followed Florida law and reflected genuine operational needs.

"The requirements in our specification document came directly from the people who will use this system every day — finance staff, HR professionals, department heads," Moreno wrote. "We make no apologies for being specific about what we need. Vague requirements lead to failed implementations."

Moreno declined a request for an in-person interview. Lowenstein, the IT director, did not respond to multiple phone and email messages.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who voted to approve the contract in March, said he had no concerns about the sole-source process.

"Tyler is the gold standard for municipal ERP," Bergosh said in a phone interview. "Half the counties in Florida use them. We're not reinventing the wheel here."

Asked whether the board had considered requiring competitive bids, Bergosh said staff had assured commissioners that sole-source was appropriate.

"I trust our professionals," he said. "That's why we hire them."

A pattern across Florida?

Tyler Technologies has secured at least 12 sole-source ERP contracts with Florida local governments since 2020, according to a Flightline review of public procurement records. The company's Munis platform now runs financial and human resources systems in 34 of Florida's 67 counties.

Tyler spokesperson Jordan Mitchell said in an email that the company "competes vigorously for every opportunity" and wins contracts "based on the strength of our solutions and our track record of successful implementations."

"Local governments choose Tyler because we deliver," Mitchell wrote. "Our Florida references speak for themselves."

The company reported $2.1 billion in revenue in 2025, with local government ERP systems accounting for approximately 40% of its business, according to SEC filings.

What the critics say

Ben Wilcox, research director at the nonprofit government watchdog Integrity Florida, said sole-source contracts deserve extra scrutiny even when they're legally permissible.

"The question isn't just whether it's legal. It's whether taxpayers are getting the best value," Wilcox said. "When you write specifications that only one vendor can meet, you've eliminated the market discipline that competitive bidding provides. Maybe Tyler was the best choice. But now we'll never know."

Wilcox said his organization has tracked a statewide increase in sole-source technology contracts since 2020, a trend he attributes partly to the complexity of modern government software.

"These systems are complicated. It's genuinely hard to compare vendors," he said. "But that's exactly why you need competition — to force vendors to explain why their solution is worth the money."

The money trail

The $2.1 million contract covers software licensing, implementation services, data migration, and three years of support. Annual maintenance after that period will cost approximately $280,000, according to contract documents.

The county's 2009 SAP implementation cost $1.4 million. Adjusted for inflation, that's roughly $2.1 million — meaning the county is paying about the same in real dollars for the replacement.

But direct cost comparisons are difficult. The original SAP system was installed on county-owned servers. The Tyler system will run in the cloud, eliminating hardware costs but creating permanent subscription dependencies.

"You're trading capital expense for operating expense," said Rachel Torres, a technology analyst with the Florida League of Cities. "That can make sense, but boards need to understand they're committing to those payments essentially forever. It's not a one-time purchase."

The contract includes no cap on future price increases after the initial three-year term.

What happens next

Tyler is scheduled to begin implementation in September 2026, with full deployment expected by July 2027. The rollout will affect every county department that handles money or personnel — effectively the entire government.

Commissioners will receive quarterly progress updates, according to the contract. The first is due in December.

Whether the board will revisit its procurement procedures remains unclear. Commissioner Bergosh said he saw no need for changes.

"We followed the law," he said. "That's the standard."

Wilcox disagreed.

"Following the law is the floor, not the ceiling," he said. "The question is whether Escambia County wants to do better than the minimum. Right now, the answer appears to be no."

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Three years after Hurricane Sally, Pensacola Beach rebuilding permits have slowed to a trickle
articles.dek: New construction dominated the first two years of recovery. Now, with insurance costs tripling and contractor shortages persisting, property owners are selling lots instead of rebuilding.
brief: Escambia County issued just 12 residential building permits on Pensacola Beach in the first six months of 2026, compared to 87 during the same period in 2024.
Insurance premiums for beach properties have increased an average of 218% since Hurricane Sally, pricing out many longtime property owners.
Real estate listings for vacant lots on the beach have tripled since January, as owners choose to sell rather than rebuild.
articles.body:
The concrete slab at 1847 Via de Luna sits empty. Rebar stubs poke through the surface like broken fingers. A faded permit notice from 2022 still clings to a wooden stake at the lot's edge, the plastic sleeve clouded by three years of salt air and sun.

Linda Marchetti paid $40,000 to have her hurricane-damaged home demolished. She spent another $15,000 on architectural plans. The permits were approved. Then her insurance renewal arrived.

"I just stopped," Marchetti said. "I couldn't do it."

Her premium had jumped from $4,200 a year to $14,800. The quote for the new construction came in at $22,000 annually—for a home she hadn't built yet.

Marchetti listed the lot for sale in March. She's one of dozens of Pensacola Beach property owners who started the rebuilding process after Hurricane Sally and never finished.

The numbers tell the story

Escambia County building permit data shows a stark reversal in beach construction activity. In 2024, the county issued 87 residential building permits for properties on Pensacola Beach between January and June. In 2025, that number fell to 41. This year, through June 30, the county has issued just 12.

"The surge is over," said Marcus Webb, director of Escambia County's Development Services Department. "What you're seeing now is closer to normal, maybe even below normal."

Webb said the initial wave of permits reflected insurance payouts from Sally, which made landfall in September 2020 as a Category 2 hurricane. The storm caused an estimated $7.3 billion in damage across the Gulf Coast, with Pensacola Beach among the hardest-hit areas.

Properties that were total losses qualified for full replacement coverage. Owners had money in hand and motivation to rebuild.

"For the first 18 months, we were processing permits as fast as they came in," Webb said. "Contractors were booked solid. Everyone wanted to get back."

That momentum has stalled.

Insurance becomes the barrier

The Florida Office of Insurance Regulation does not publish premium data by municipality, but local insurance agents describe a market in crisis.

Tom Fitzgerald has sold property insurance in Pensacola for 31 years. His office on Gregory Street handles roughly 200 beach policies. He said the average annual premium for a single-family home on Pensacola Beach was approximately $3,800 before Sally. Today, that same coverage costs between $11,000 and $16,000.

"And that's if you can get it," Fitzgerald said. "I've got clients who've been dropped by three carriers in two years."

Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, the state-backed insurer of last resort, has become the primary carrier for many beach properties. Citizens premiums have increased 45% since 2023 under a state-mandated "glide path" intended to bring rates closer to private market levels.

For new construction, the numbers are worse. Insurers assess new builds based on current replacement costs, which have climbed sharply with materials and labor prices. A 2,400-square-foot home that would have cost $380,000 to build in 2020 now runs closer to $520,000, according to estimates from the National Association of Home Builders.

Higher replacement costs mean higher premiums.

Fitzgerald said several of his clients have abandoned building plans specifically because of insurance quotes.

"They've got the lot. They've got the financing. They've got the plans," he said. "Then they see what the insurance will cost every year for the next 30 years, and they walk."

Contractors have moved on

The insurance problem compounds another: there aren't enough people to do the work.

Gulf Coast Builders, one of the larger residential contractors operating on Pensacola Beach, employed 34 construction workers in early 2024. Owner Ray Stokes said he's down to 19.

"Guys went to Louisiana after the storms there. Some went to Texas," Stokes said. "The work here dried up, and they followed the money."

Stokes said his company completed 11 beach homes in 2024. This year, they've finished two, with three more under construction. He has not taken a new beach project since February.

"It's not that people don't want to build," he said. "It's that by the time they get their financing and their insurance sorted out, six months have passed. Then they come back and I tell them I can't start for another eight months. A lot of them give up."

The Pensacola Association of Building Contractors reported in May that its membership has declined 12% since 2024. Executive Director Paula Henning attributed the drop partly to contractors retiring or relocating, and partly to smaller firms closing after the post-Sally boom ended.

The lots go up for sale

Pensacola Beach real estate agent Darren Kinsley pulled the listing data on his laptop at a coffee shop on Quietwater Beach Road. He scrolled through pages of vacant lot listings.

"Thirty-seven active listings for vacant residential lots as of this morning," Kinsley said. "This time last year, there were maybe twelve."

Listing prices range from $180,000 for interior lots to over $1.2 million for Gulf-front parcels. Many of the listings note "permits approved" or "plans available."

Kinsley said the buyers are changing too. Five years ago, most purchasers planned to build primary or secondary residences. Now, he estimates 60% of his lot buyers are investors or developers.

"They're buying and holding, or they're aggregating parcels," he said. "The individual family that wants to build their beach house—those calls have basically stopped."

The shift concerns some longtime residents.

Susan Haas has owned a home on Ariola Drive since 1994. She watched her neighbors' houses come down after Sally. She watched the rebuilding start. Now she watches the lots accumulate.

"This used to be a neighborhood," Haas said. "People knew each other. We had block parties. Now half the street is empty dirt and 'For Sale' signs."

Haas said she worries about what the beach will look like when—or if—the building resumes.

"The houses they're building now, they're enormous," she said. "Three stories, rental pools, the whole setup. That's not a neighborhood. That's a hotel district."

County officials watch and wait

Santa Rosa Island Authority General Manager Paolo Ghio said the permitting slowdown has not significantly affected the authority's budget, which draws revenue primarily from lease fees rather than construction activity. But he acknowledged the stalled rebuilding creates other problems.

"Empty lots don't contribute to the community," Ghio said. "They don't support local businesses. They don't have residents who participate in island governance."

The authority has no mechanism to compel property owners to build. Lease agreements require lessees to maintain their properties, but an empty, maintained lot satisfies that requirement.

Ghio said the authority is monitoring the situation but has not proposed any policy changes.

At the county level, Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said the insurance crisis requires state and federal solutions.

"This is not something Escambia County can fix," Bergosh said in an email response to questions. "We need comprehensive reform of the property insurance market in Florida, and we need it now."

Bergosh did not respond to follow-up questions about specific reforms he supports.

Marchetti weighs her options

Back on Via de Luna, Linda Marchetti has received one offer on her lot. It came from an LLC registered in Delaware. The offer was $60,000 below her asking price.

She turned it down.

"I'm not desperate yet," she said. "But ask me again in six months."

Marchetti, 67, is a retired teacher from Mobile. She bought the Pensacola Beach house in 2008 as a vacation property, then moved in full-time after her husband died in 2017. Sally took the roof and most of the second floor.

She lives in a rented condo in Gulf Breeze now. The view is of a parking lot.

"I thought I'd spend the rest of my life on that beach," she said. "I had the spot picked out where I wanted my ashes scattered. It sounds morbid, but that's how much I loved it there."

She visits the lot sometimes. She parks on the street and looks at the slab.

"Maybe if insurance gets better," she said. "Maybe if I win the lottery."

She laughed, but it wasn't a happy sound.

"I just didn't think it would end like this."

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's summer training surge puts 4,000 extra bodies on base—and downtown
articles.dek: July marks peak season for aviation students rotating through the cradle of naval aviation. Local bars, landlords, and traffic patterns feel the weight.
brief: Naval Air Station Pensacola hosts approximately 4,000 additional student naval aviators and flight officers during peak summer training months
Local businesses along Palafox Street report 30-40% revenue increases during summer training surge, while landlords in East Hill and downtown see near-zero vacancy rates
Base officials and city traffic engineers are coordinating on gate access and signal timing to manage increased vehicle flow on Navy Boulevard and Blue Angel Parkway
articles.body:
The line at Intermission starts forming at 2147 on a Thursday. Twenty-three naval flight students in polo shirts and boat shoes crowd the sidewalk on South Palafox, checking watches. Liberty expires at midnight. They have two hours and thirteen minutes to drink.

"Summer's our Super Bowl," said Marcus Webb, a bartender at the downtown cocktail bar. "Rest of the year it's steady. June through August, we're slammed five nights a week."

Naval Air Station Pensacola—the cradle of naval aviation since 1914—runs year-round flight training. But summer brings the surge. Approximately 4,000 additional student naval aviators, student naval flight officers, and Marine Corps aviation students rotate through the installation between Memorial Day and Labor Day, according to base public affairs. They join the roughly 16,000 military personnel already assigned to NAS Pensacola and its tenant commands.

The impact ripples outward from the base gates.

The housing squeeze

Student aviators are not required to live on base. Most don't. They rent apartments in East Hill, condos downtown, houses in the neighborhoods hugging Bayou Texar. They pay market rate, often splitting three or four to a unit.

"I haven't had a vacancy longer than seventy-two hours since April," said Jennifer Coulter, who manages twelve rental properties within two miles of NAS Pensacola's main gate. "I could charge more. I don't, because I want the Navy tenants. They pay on time. They deploy. They leave."

Coulter said she maintains a waiting list of incoming students referred by outgoing ones. The informal network moves faster than any listing service.

For non-military renters, the competition stings. Average rent for a one-bedroom apartment in the 32501 and 32502 ZIP codes climbed to $1,340 per month in June 2026, according to Zillow data—up 8.2% from the same period last year. Pensacola's median household income sits at $54,800, per the most recent Census Bureau estimates.

"It's supply and demand," said Escambia County Property Appraiser Chris Jones. "You've got a guaranteed influx of renters with steady paychecks every single summer. Landlords know it."

Bars, restaurants, and the liberty economy

Flight students operate under strict conduct codes. Alcohol incidents can end careers before they start. But the rules don't prohibit drinking—they regulate it. And downtown Pensacola's bar district has oriented itself accordingly.

O'Riley's Irish Pub on Government Street hosts "Aviator Night" every Wednesday. Half-price wells for anyone with a military ID. The promotion has run for eleven years.

"These kids are going to be fighter pilots, helicopter pilots, guys landing on aircraft carriers," said O'Riley's owner Patrick Shea. "They're also twenty-three years old and away from home. They want to blow off steam. We'd rather they do it somewhere safe."

Shea estimates naval aviation students account for 35-40% of his summer revenue. He's not alone. A informal survey of eight downtown bars and restaurants conducted by The Flightline found all reported measurable increases in summer business attributed to military customers. Estimates ranged from 20% to 50% of seasonal revenue.

The relationship is symbiotic but occasionally tense. In 2024, a brawl between flight students and civilians at a Palafox Street bar resulted in two arrests and a temporary off-limits designation for the establishment. The designation—which prohibits military personnel from patronizing a business—was lifted after sixty days.

"One incident in how many years?" Shea said. "These are good kids. They're not the problem."

Traffic patterns and gate math

Every weekday morning between 0630 and 0730, Navy Boulevard becomes a parking lot.

The main gate at NAS Pensacola processes roughly 12,000 vehicle entries per day during normal operations, according to base public affairs. During summer training surge, that number climbs to approximately 15,500. The math is unforgiving. More cars. Same gates. Same hours.

"We've added additional gate guards during peak hours and opened auxiliary lanes when possible," said Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Torres, NAS Pensacola's public affairs officer. "We also encourage personnel to adjust their schedules when mission requirements allow."

The city of Pensacola has been less flexible. Traffic signals along Navy Boulevard are timed for normal flow. Adjusting them for summer surge would disrupt civilian commuter patterns on a road that serves multiple schools and commercial districts.

"We're in conversations with the base about signal timing and alternative routing," said Pensacola City Council member Allison Patton, whose District 6 includes much of the area surrounding NAS Pensacola. "It's complicated. That's a city road serving city residents. But we also recognize the base is our largest employer."

Patton said the city and base have discussed a pilot program to adjust signal timing during June, July, and August mornings. No decision has been made.

The economics of the cradle

NAS Pensacola generates an estimated $5.1 billion in annual economic impact for the Pensacola metropolitan area, according to a 2024 study commissioned by the Florida Defense Alliance. The figure includes direct military payroll, contractor spending, retiree benefits, and induced economic activity.

The summer surge adds approximately $47 million to that total, the study found—a figure driven primarily by housing expenditures, food and beverage spending, and vehicle-related costs.

"People talk about tourism," said Scott Luth, president and CEO of FloridaWest Economic Development Alliance. "And tourism matters. But the military is the foundation. It's been the foundation since before anyone alive today was born."

The relationship shapes the region in ways both visible and invisible. Flight students who pass through Pensacola often return—as instructors, as retirees, as civilians who remember the Gulf Coast fondly.

"I came here for flight school in 2009," said retired Navy Cmdr. David Reyes, who now runs a consulting firm in Gulf Breeze. "Met my wife at a bar on Palafox. Bought a house in 2019. It happens more than people realize."

The view from the line

Back at Intermission, the Thursday night crowd has thinned. It's 2315. Liberty ends in forty-five minutes. The flight students settle their tabs in cash, tip generously, check their watches again.

"Pensacola's great," said a student naval aviator who asked to be identified only by his call sign, "Wedge." He's twenty-four, from Ohio, three months into primary flight training. "The flying is hard. The ground school is harder. But the town's cool. People are nice. The beach is right there."

He paused.

"Ask me again after I solo," he said. "If I solo."

He checked his watch one more time. Then he walked out into the Pensacola night, toward the base, toward the flight line, toward whatever comes next.
